title: Vienna 1900: The Secession and the Diaries
subtitle: The Secession, Klimt, Mahler, Freud and Schoenberg, Vienna, 1897–1914
intro: Between the founding of the Secession in April 1897 and the summer of 1914, Vienna produced, in a few square kilometres, new painting, new architecture and design, a new music and a new theory of the mind. The people who made them dined at the same tables, read the same newspapers and attended the same openings. This chapter lays their records side by side: the paintings and the reviews, the concert and the next morning's gossip, the dinner and the diary entry written that night.

The honest record is uneven. Arthur Schnitzler kept a near-daily diary for fifty years, and Alma Schindler kept one through her courtships of 1898 to 1902; both were published only in the late twentieth century and are digested here, never quoted. Klimt, the painter at the centre of the storm, left little more than postcards. Most of the other voices are dated letters (Mahler, Freud, Schoenberg), dated newspaper criticism (Hevesi, Bahr) and a satirist's journal (Kraus's Die Fackel). Berta Zuckerkandl, whose salon brought many of them together, wrote her account in exile in 1939 and is marked as memoir.

The first great clash came in March 1900, when Klimt's Philosophy, painted for the ceiling of the university, went on show at the Secession. Professors petitioned against it, critics fought for and against it for weeks, and it went on to win a Grand Prix in Paris. A few months earlier Freud had published The Interpretation of Dreams to near silence. The two works argued, in different languages, that reason was not the master of the house.

The rooms are the heart of the chapter: the Zuckerkandl dinner in November 1901 where Alma Schindler, seated beside her former suitor Klimt, met Mahler; the Beethoven exhibition of April 1902, where painting, sculpture, architecture and Mahler's trombones were meant to make one artwork; the Kunstschau of 1908, where the state bought The Kiss; and the Musikverein on 31 March 1913, where Schoenberg's concert ended in a brawl.

Several famous moments survive only as anecdote: Klimt's word on the station platform as Mahler left, Alma's later versions of her marriage, the hostess's memory of the first meeting. They are marked as such. What the contemporary record shows is a city in which a handful of people produced work that was greeted, almost every time, with laughter, petitions and lawsuits, and which they defended by talking, writing and exhibiting together.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian; Austria-Hungary used the Gregorian calendar throughout this period.

eyes.name: Arthur Schnitzler
eyes.role: Physician turned playwright and novelist, aged 35 in 1897; author of Reigen and Leutnant Gustl
eyes.vantage_label: the diarist in the stalls and at the dinner table
eyes.authenticity: Schnitzler kept a daily diary from 1879 until two days before his death. It was published by the Austrian Academy of Sciences in ten volumes (1981–2000) and is now a free digital edition with a linked day-by-day chronicle. Modern publication: digested here, never quoted.
eyes.bio: The most regular eye in the chapter: a near-daily record of rehearsals, concerts, dinners and walks, laconic and often sharp. He was rarely at the centre of the art scandals, which is exactly why his diary shows how they looked from a few rows back.

sources.title: Schnitzler Tagebuch digital edition and chronicle (ÖAW/ACDH)

eyes.name: Alma Maria Schindler (later Mahler)
eyes.role: Daughter of the landscape painter Emil Jakob Schindler and stepdaughter of the Secession founder Carl Moll; trained composer, aged 19–22 in her diary years
eyes.side: The Moll household on the Hohe Warte; Secession circle
eyes.where: Hohe Warte, Vienna; Italy in spring 1899; from March 1902 the Mahler household
eyes.vantage_label: the young woman at the dinner table and in the diary
eyes.authenticity: The diaries she kept from 1898 to 1902 survive in manuscript and were published only in 1997 (German edition ed. Beaumont and Rode-Breymann; English 'Diaries 1898–1902'). Her later memoirs (Gustav Mahler: Erinnerungen und Briefe, 1940; Mein Leben, 1960) were written decades afterwards and are widely regarded as unreliable and self-serving; they are not used as diary evidence here. Modern publication: digest only.
eyes.bio: Alma's diaries are the rare inside record of the Secession's private life written by a young woman who was courted by Klimt and then by Mahler, and who was herself composing. They show the men of 1900 from across the table rather than from the gallery wall.

sources.title: Gustav Mahler and Alma Schindler: their six-week courtship (Interlude)

eyes.name: Gustav Klimt
eyes.role: Painter, aged 34 at the founding of the Secession and its first president; commissioned in 1894 to paint ceiling panels for the University of Vienna
eyes.where: Studio in Josefstädter Straße, Vienna; summers on the Attersee
eyes.vantage_label: the painter at the storm's centre
eyes.form: postcards and letters; dated works and exhibition records
eyes.authenticity: Klimt kept no diary and wrote little. About 400 postcards and letters to Emilie Flöge survive (now at the Leopold Museum); many are brief and some undated. His public record is mostly exhibition catalogues, guest books and the press. Spoken remarks attributed to him by others are anecdotes, not documents.
eyes.bio: The man most of the other eyes were looking at. His own voice survives mainly in terse postcards, which makes the contrast with the torrent of print about him one of the chapter's subjects.

eyes.name: Gustav Mahler
eyes.role: Director of the Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907, composer; aged 41 when he met Alma Schindler
eyes.side: Court Opera; friend of the Secession artists
eyes.where: Court Opera, Vienna; summers at Maiernigg; New York from Dec 1907
eyes.authenticity: Mahler's letters survive in large numbers and are edited (to Alma, ed. Beaumont; collected letters ed. Blaukopf). Alma's own 1940 edition of his letters to her was cut and altered; modern editions restore the texts. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Mahler was the establishment and the avant-garde at once: the Emperor's opera director and the composer whose symphonies split audiences. His letters show the cost of both roles.

eyes.name: Sigmund Freud
eyes.role: Neurologist in private practice at Berggasse 19, aged 43 when The Interpretation of Dreams appeared; Privatdozent at the University
eyes.vantage_label: the neighbour in the consulting room
eyes.authenticity: Freud's letters to the Berlin physician Wilhelm Fliess survived because Fliess's widow sold them; Marie Bonaparte bought them in 1937. A selection appeared in 1950 and the complete letters, ed. Masson, in 1985. Modern translation: digest only.
eyes.bio: Freud's book and the Secession's paintings appeared in the same months and the same university; his letters record the silence that met the dream book while the city argued about Klimt's ceiling.

sources.title: History of Information: publication of Die Traumdeutung

eyes.name: Hermann Bahr
eyes.role: Critic, playwright and impresario of 'Young Vienna'; the Secession's loudest literary champion
eyes.where: Vienna; villa in Ober St. Veit designed by Olbrich
eyes.form: criticism, lectures and an anthology of attacks
eyes.authenticity: Bahr's essays and lectures were printed in his lifetime (Secession, 1900; Rede über Klimt, 1901; Gegen Klimt, 1903). His diaries and notebooks are being edited (Csáky et al., from 1994) but are not used here day by day.
eyes.bio: Bahr turned criticism into a campaign: he bought Klimt's Nuda Veritas in 1900, lectured in his defence, and in 1903 published the hostile press as a book, letting the attacks condemn themselves.

sources.title: Bahr on Klimt, Universität Wien Bahr project (PDF)

eyes.name: Karl Kraus
eyes.role: Satirist, aged 25 when he founded and wrote Die Fackel
eyes.side: Independent; enemy of Bahr and of the Secession's press friends
eyes.vantage_label: the satirist with his own journal
eyes.authenticity: Die Fackel ran from 1 April 1899 to 1936, 922 numbers, almost all by Kraus. The full run is freely searchable in the Austrian Academy's AAC-Fackel edition. Issue numbers give month-level dates.
eyes.bio: Kraus is the hostile eye: he attacked Klimt's Philosophy, its defenders and the newspapers that praised it. He also later championed Loos, Kokoschka and Schoenberg, so his hostility was aimed at the Secession's alliance with the press rather than at new art as such.

eyes.name: Ludwig Hevesi
eyes.role: Hungarian-born art critic of the Fremden-Blatt and Pester Lloyd, in his mid-fifties when the Secession began
eyes.authenticity: Hevesi's reviews appeared in daily papers and were collected by him in Acht Jahre Secession (1906) and Altkunst – Neukunst (1909), with their dates. He died in Vienna in February 1910.
eyes.bio: Hevesi wrote the motto over the Secession's door and reviewed nearly every exhibition on opening day. His dated feuilletons are the nearest thing the movement has to a diary.

sources.title: Index Journal: the 1900 press campaigns around the Faculty Paintings

eyes.name: Berta Zuckerkandl
eyes.role: Journalist and salon hostess, wife of the anatomist Emil Zuckerkandl; art writer for the Wiener Allgemeine Zeitung
eyes.vantage_label: the hostess who seated the guests
eyes.authenticity: Her press articles are dated. Her memoir Ich erlebte fünfzig Jahre Weltgeschichte (1939) was written in exile nearly forty years after the events and is flagged as memoir. She fled Vienna in 1938.
eyes.bio: Zuckerkandl's salon is where the eyes physically met: Klimt, Mahler, Alma, Schnitzler, Moll. She wrote about the Secession as a journalist and, much later, as a witness remembering.

sources.title: Gustav Klimt and the 1908 Kunstschau (Google Arts & Culture)

eyes.name: Arnold Schoenberg
eyes.role: Composer and teacher, largely self-taught, aged 23 in 1897; teacher of Berg and Webern
eyes.vantage_label: the composer the hall turned on
eyes.form: dated letters, interviews and dated paintings
eyes.authenticity: Schoenberg's letters, paintings and papers are held by the Arnold Schönberg Center, Vienna. His newspaper interview after the 1913 concert is dated. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Schoenberg carried the Secession's argument from walls into sound. Mahler protected him; Kraus admired him; the Vienna concert public, in 1908 and 1913, did not.

eyes.name: Josef Hoffmann
eyes.role: Architect and designer, aged 26 at the Secession's founding; co-founder of the Wiener Werkstätte with Koloman Moser and Fritz Waerndorfer
eyes.form: dated designs, institutional records and programmes
eyes.authenticity: Hoffmann's drawings and the Wiener Werkstätte archive are held by the MAK, Vienna. The WW work programme (1905) and commercial registry entries are dated documents; Hoffmann kept no diary.
eyes.bio: Hoffmann designed the spaces in which the others' work was seen, from Secession installations to the Purkersdorf sanatorium and the Palais Stoclet. He stands here for the craftsmen and designers whose names were on the programmes.

eyes.name: Heinrich Schenker
eyes.role: Music theorist, editor and teacher, aged 44 in 1913
eyes.side: Conservative musical Vienna; opponent of Schoenberg's direction
eyes.authenticity: Schenker's diaries (from 1896, near-daily from 1912) survive at the New York Public Library and the Oswald Jonas collection, UC Riverside; they are being transcribed and translated by Schenker Documents Online. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Schenker hated what Schoenberg stood for, but his diary shows that he learned of the 1913 scandal the next morning through his household's talk, like most of Vienna.

entries.headline: Nineteen artists found the Vereinigung: the Secession
entries.digest: A group of nineteen artists, with Klimt at their head, founded the Union of Austrian Artists while still members of the Künstlerhaus, the conservative body that ran Vienna's exhibitions. Klimt was chosen as president. The break with the Künstlerhaus became formal that spring; the founders' aim was exhibitions of living art, foreign as well as Austrian, without the old hanging committees.
entries.source_note: History Today, 'The Vienna Secession is Founded' (3 April 1897); Klimt-Database biography.

entries.headline: The 'golden cabbage' opens with his motto over the door
entries.digest: Olbrich's white building with its gilded laurel dome opened with the second exhibition. Over the entrance stood Hevesi's own motto, 'To every age its art, to art its freedom.' Hevesi greeted it as a temple for a new Vienna; the popular nicknames, such as the gilded cabbage, came from less friendly mouths.
entries.quote: Der Zeit ihre Kunst, der Kunst ihre Freiheit
entries.source_note: Vienna Secession building page (opening 12 Nov 1898, Hevesi motto); Hevesi's review collected in Acht Jahre Secession (1906), review day not checked.

entries.headline: Pallas Athene in the new building
entries.digest: Klimt showed his Pallas Athene at the second exhibition: the goddess in gilded armour, holding a small naked figure of Truth. It worked as an emblem for the young association, wisdom armed and facing out, and it hung inside the building whose opening Klimt's group had paid for with the first show's takings.
entries.source_note: Exhibition opening date verified (Secession building page); the inclusion of Pallas Athene from standard catalogues.

entries.headline: The first red number of Die Fackel
entries.digest: Kraus launched his own journal, in a red cover, after the Neues Wiener Tagblatt announced it on 30 March. It was meant to light up the corruption of the press and the cliques of literary Vienna, Bahr's included. Thousands of copies sold in the first days.
entries.source_note: Austria-Forum, Die Fackel (Erstausgabe 1 April 1899; NWT announcement 30 March 1899).

entries.headline: Klimt in Italy, and her stepfather's anger
entries.digest: Klimt joined the Moll family on a ten-day Italian journey that included Florence, Genoa, Verona and Venice. Alma's diary records his courtship and a kiss; when Carl Moll discovered it he confronted Klimt, and the two founders of the Secession nearly fell out before making peace back in Vienna. Alma wrote of being in love and of her own confusion.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database 'Italy' (spring 1899 trip, Moll's discovery); Alma Mahler-Werfel, Diaries 1898–1902 (1997). Exact days not verified.

entries.headline: Only two copies of the dream book exist
entries.digest: Freud thanked Fliess for his kind response to the copy of the dream book he had sent ahead of publication. The book had not yet been issued; Freud remarked that only their two copies had so far seen daylight. His own presentation copy for Fliess carried a date of 24 October.
entries.source_note: Freud to Fliess, 27 Oct 1899 (Masson ed. 1985), as cited by History of Information.

entries.headline: Die Traumdeutung appears, dated 1900
entries.digest: The Interpretation of Dreams went on sale in Vienna and Leipzig with the year 1900 on its title page, a publisher's choice for the new century. The first printing of 600 copies took years to sell. Freud expected silence from the medical faculty and largely got it.
entries.source_note: Jones, Sigmund Freud I, as cited by History of Information (4 Nov 1899; title page 1900).

entries.headline: Kraus: who cares how Klimt imagines philosophy?
entries.digest: In Fackel number 36 Kraus wrote his first attack on the painting, under the plain title 'Klimt'. He did not much argue about the brushwork; he mocked the idea that a painter's private allegory should decorate the university, and he went after the critics who were organising praise for it.
entries.source_note: Die Fackel, H. 36 (1900), pp. 16–20, per Klimt-Database 'Karl Kraus' and Index Journal.

entries.headline: Hevesi praises Philosophy on opening day
entries.digest: The seventh Secession exhibition opened with Klimt's Philosophy, the first of the three ceiling paintings for the university, at its centre: a column of naked bodies drifting through a starry void, a dim face of Knowledge below. Hevesi's review appeared the same day and treated it as a cosmic vision.
entries.source_note: Index Journal, '1900—Pyrrhic Victory' (opening and Hevesi review 8 March 1900).

entries.headline: Philosophy goes on the wall, and the storm begins
entries.digest: Klimt's first faculty painting was meant to celebrate philosophy on the ceiling of the university's Great Hall. Instead of a triumph of reason it showed humanity carried along by blind forces. Critics split within days, and by late March leading Secession members laid a laurel wreath before it bearing Hevesi's motto.
entries.source_note: Index Journal chronology (8 March opening; 27 March wreath); Austria-Forum, Fakultätsbilder.

entries.headline: The newspapers name it an 'agitation'
entries.digest: The Neue Freie Presse reported on the agitation against Klimt's Philosophy among university professors. Within days Hevesi answered in the Fremden-Blatt with pieces defending Klimt and mocking the 'image-breakers of Vienna'. He saw the protest as philistines against art; his opponents saw a critic who had appointed himself spokesman.
entries.source_note: Neue Freie Presse 26 March 1900 p.3 (Univ. Wien '650 plus' record); Index Journal (Hevesi in Fremden-Blatt 28 March, 'Für Klimt', 'Die Bilderstürmer von Wien').

entries.headline: Bahr lectures in defence of Philosophy
entries.digest: Bahr gave a public lecture defending the painting, which was printed and passed around as a manifesto. He answered the professors with irony rather than argument, and that same year he bought Klimt's Nuda Veritas for himself, a painting inscribed with a warning about pleasing the many.
entries.source_note: Index Journal (Bahr's lecture, undated); Klimt-Database 'Hermann Bahr' (purchase of Nuda Veritas, 1900).

entries.headline: A second attack, aimed at Hevesi and at Paris
entries.digest: As Philosophy travelled to Paris and won a Grand Prix at the World's Fair, Kraus attacked again in number 41, now chiefly at Hevesi. He sneered at the idea that Parisian approval proved anything, using an ethnic jibe of the kind common in Viennese polemic at the time.
entries.source_note: Index Journal (Fackel no. 41, May 1900).

entries.headline: Imagining a marble tablet
entries.digest: Writing to Fliess from the Bellevue house on the hills above Vienna, Freud wondered whether a marble tablet would one day mark the place where the secret of dreams had revealed itself to him in July 1895. He added that he saw little prospect of it. The book had sold poorly and had hardly been reviewed.
entries.source_note: Freud to Fliess, 12 June 1900, as cited by Freud Quotes blog; a plaque now stands at the site.

entries.headline: First summer on the Attersee
entries.digest: Klimt signed the guest book of the Villa Paulick on the Attersee during his first summer holiday there with the Flöge family. He would return for seventeen summers, painting square landscapes of water and trees far from the university quarrel.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database biography (guest book signature 10 Aug 1900).

entries.headline: Leutnant Gustl appears in the Christmas paper
entries.digest: Schnitzler's novella, written entirely as the panicked inner monologue of a young officer who has been insulted by a baker and thinks he must shoot himself, appeared in the Christmas supplement of the Neue Freie Presse. It mocked the army's code of honour from inside an officer's head.
entries.source_note: Publication in the NFP Christmas number 1900 is standard; day not checked against the paper.

entries.headline: The Rede über Klimt
entries.digest: Medicine, the second faculty painting, opened at the tenth Secession exhibition and provoked questions in parliament and the confiscation of an issue of Ver Sacrum for its drawings. Bahr spoke on Klimt before the writers' association Concordia, and the speech was printed as a pamphlet.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database 'Hermann Bahr' (Rede über Klimt at Concordia, 1901; Concordia evening reported NFP 26 March 1901, link to the speech not confirmed).

entries.headline: Stripped of his officer's rank
entries.digest: An army court of honour ruled that Schnitzler, a reserve medical officer, had damaged the officer corps' honour with Leutnant Gustl and had failed to answer attacks on it in the press. He lost his commission. He did not contest it.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts give 14 June 1901 for the ruling; not checked against the diary.

entries.headline: Seated between Klimt and Burckhard, opposite Mahler
entries.digest: At Berta Zuckerkandl's dinner Alma sat between Klimt and the theatre director Max Burckhard, facing Mahler. She argued with Mahler about a ballet score by her teacher Zemlinsky that he had not answered, and found him sharp and attractive. Her diary that night recorded the meeting at length.
entries.source_note: Interlude, 'Gustav Mahler and Alma Schindler: their six-week whirlwind courtship' (7 Nov 1901, seating); Diaries 1898–1902.

entries.headline: The hostess remembers the evening
entries.digest: In her memoir written nearly four decades later, Zuckerkandl described bringing Mahler to a small dinner and watching him engage the young Alma Schindler. Her account is the hostess's version, shaped by hindsight: by then the evening had become the opening of a famous marriage.
entries.source_note: Berta Zuckerkandl, Ich erlebte fünfzig Jahre Weltgeschichte (1939). Memoir, written later.

entries.headline: Mahler at the dinner table
entries.digest: Mahler, who avoided society, came to the Zuckerkandls' dinner and met Alma Schindler. The next morning he invited her and the Zuckerkandl women to a dress rehearsal at the Court Opera, and on 11 November she attended his premiere of The Tales of Hoffmann.
entries.source_note: Interlude (dinner 7 Nov; rehearsal invitation next morning; Hoffmann 11 Nov 1901).

entries.headline: The letter that asked her to stop composing
entries.digest: From a concert tour in Dresden Mahler wrote Alma a long letter setting terms for their marriage: there could be only one composer in the house, and her role would be to live for his work. He asked for her answer before they met again.
entries.source_note: Interlude (letter of 19 Dec 1901 from Dresden). Mahler's letters to Alma, ed. Beaumont.

entries.headline: Engaged
entries.digest: Alma accepted Mahler. Her diary recorded both the joy and the sense of what she was giving up; she had wept over the Dresden letter but decided to submit to its terms. The engagement was announced in the newspapers on 27 December.
entries.source_note: Interlude (engagement and diary entry 23 Dec; press announcement 27 Dec 1901).

entries.headline: Married in the sacristy
entries.digest: Alma Schindler and Gustav Mahler married quietly in the sacristy of the Karlskirche at 1.30 p.m.; she was already pregnant. Her diary, which had followed her since 1898, petered out soon afterwards.
entries.source_note: Interlude (wedding 9 March 1902, Karlskirche sacristy, 1.30 p.m.).

entries.headline: Freud becomes a professor, and says how
entries.digest: After years of waiting, Freud was named extraordinary professor. He told Fliess, in what proved one of the last letters of their friendship, that the title had come through patronage and his own giving in, not merit, and described the congratulations with heavy irony.
entries.source_note: Freud to Fliess, 11 March 1902 (Masson ed.); date standard but not checked in this session.

entries.headline: Designing the Beethoven rooms
entries.digest: Hoffmann designed the exhibition's installation, a sequence of austere rooms leading to the central hall, with abstract relief panels of his own above the doors. The whole show was treated as one artwork, painting, sculpture, architecture and, on opening night, music.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts of the 14th exhibition; Hoffmann's role from MAK and Secession sources, not checked in detail.

entries.headline: Six trombones on the staircase
entries.digest: On the evening before the private view of the fourteenth Secession exhibition, devoted to Beethoven and built around Max Klinger's marble statue, Mahler conducted his own arrangement of a passage from the Ninth Symphony's choral finale. It was played from the vestibule staircase by six trombones and lasted a few minutes; the audience was invited.
entries.source_note: Mahler Foundation, Chronology 1902 (14 April, evening before the private view, six trombones).

entries.headline: The Beethoven Frieze on the walls
entries.digest: Klimt's frieze, painted directly on the walls of the left hall, followed the longing for happiness past hostile powers to a final embrace. Visitors were led to it before reaching Klinger's Beethoven. One critic called it painted pornography; nearly 60,000 people came. The frieze was meant to be destroyed afterwards and was instead cut out and sold.
entries.source_note: Classical Music, 'The strange story of the Beethoven frieze' (visitor numbers, critic); Klimt-Database (14th exhibition).

entries.headline: Gegen Klimt: the attacks, collected
entries.digest: Bahr published a pamphlet gathering the hostile press about Klimt, with a preface of his own. The method was to let the abuse speak for itself, and it framed the whole controversy, for later readers, as reason against philistinism.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database 'Hermann Bahr' (Gegen Klimt, 1903).

entries.headline: The Wiener Werkstätte is founded
entries.digest: Hoffmann and Koloman Moser founded a cooperative of craftsmen with money from the textile heir Fritz Waerndorfer, who became its treasurer. The idea was to make every object, from cutlery to bookbindings, with the same seriousness as a painting. The Wiener Zeitung recorded it in late May.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database 'Wiener Werkstätte' (May 1903; founders; Wiener Zeitung 23 May 1903).

entries.headline: A postcard from Ravenna
entries.digest: On his second Italian journey Klimt sent Emilie Flöge a card from Ravenna, where he saw the Byzantine gold mosaics of San Vitale. The gold of his next works, the Stoclet Frieze, the Adele Bloch-Bauer portrait, The Kiss, owes much to what he saw that week.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database biography (postcard 2 Dec 1903, Ravenna; further card 10 Dec from Riva).

entries.headline: A letter to Mahler after the Third Symphony
entries.digest: After hearing Mahler conduct his Third Symphony in Vienna, Schoenberg, who had been sceptical, wrote him an effusive letter saying the music had shown him a soul laid bare. It sealed Mahler's protection of the younger composer.
entries.source_note: Mahler Foundation (Schoenberg converted by the Third Symphony); exact letter date not verified.

entries.headline: The Klimt group walks out
entries.digest: After a dispute over commercial ties to a gallery and the place of applied art, Klimt, Hoffmann, Moser and others resigned from the Secession they had founded. That year Klimt also bought back his faculty paintings and returned the state's fee, with the industrialist August Lederer's support.
entries.source_note: Vienna Secession building timeline (14 June 1905); Klimt-Database (withdrawal and repayment, 1905).

entries.headline: Hope behind the doors
entries.digest: Schnitzler and Klimt were guests of Fritz Waerndorfer, the Wiener Werkstätte's backer, and Schnitzler saw Klimt's Hope I, the painting of a pregnant nude that was considered too shocking to exhibit openly and was kept in a cabinet with doors.
entries.source_note: Schnitzler diary 22 March 1907, as cited by Klimt-Database 'Arthur Schnitzler'.

entries.headline: Leaving Vienna from the Westbahnhof
entries.digest: Mahler and Alma left Vienna by train for Paris and Cherbourg, where they sailed on 12 December for New York and the Metropolitan Opera. A crowd of friends and younger musicians came to the station to see them off; later accounts place Klimt among them. Earlier that year their elder daughter had died and Mahler had been told his heart was diseased.
entries.source_note: Mahler Foundation 'Westbahnhof' (9 Dec 1907); Classical Music 'Mahler 1907' (sailing 12 Dec; Met contract 21 June).

entries.headline: 'Over': Klimt on the platform
entries.digest: Klimt was among those who saw Mahler off. As the train pulled out he is reported to have said a single word, 'Vorbei' (over). The remark comes from later recollections of those present, not from anything Klimt wrote; it is told as anecdote.
entries.source_note: Anecdote from later accounts of the departure; not documented in Klimt's own hand.

entries.headline: Reporting the Kunstschau from the inside
entries.digest: Zuckerkandl, who had followed the Kunstschau's planning since meeting Klimt in 1907, wrote about it for the Wiener Allgemeine Zeitung. She presented it as the Klimt group's manifesto for a total Austrian art, from painting to garden and children's art.
entries.source_note: Google Arts & Culture (Zuckerkandl reported on the project in the WAZ); article date not pinned.

entries.headline: Kunstschau: room 22 and the lovers
entries.digest: The Klimt group's own exhibition opened on the empty site where the Konzerthaus would later stand. Klimt, who chaired the committee, had a room to himself with sixteen paintings, designed by Moser; the state bought the painting shown as 'Liebespaar', The Kiss, for 25,000 crowns. A young Kokoschka showed his first work in another room.
entries.source_note: Google Arts & Culture 'Gustav Klimt and the 1908 Kunstschau' (room 22, price); Wikipedia Kunstschau Wien 1908 (1 June–16 Nov).

entries.headline: Laughter at the Second Quartet
entries.digest: The Rosé Quartet, with the soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder, gave the first performance of Schoenberg's Second String Quartet, whose last movements leave key behind. Parts of the audience laughed and whistled through it; the press treated it as a scandal.
entries.source_note: Arnold Schönberg Center timeline (scandal at 1908 Vienna premiere); exact day from standard accounts.

entries.headline: Four hours with Freud
entries.digest: In a crisis over Alma's affair with the architect Walter Gropius, Mahler travelled to Leiden to see Freud, who was on holiday in the Netherlands. They walked through the town for about four hours. Freud's later account says Mahler gained insight into his attachment to his mother; Mahler wrote to Alma afterwards with renewed devotion.
entries.source_note: Meeting at Leiden, late August 1910 (commonly 26 Aug); Freud's account in a 1935 letter to Theodor Reik (later).

entries.headline: The composer on a walk
entries.digest: Freud interrupted his holiday to meet Mahler, who had cancelled appointments several times. Freud later remembered the conversation as an analysis carried out on a walk, the only treatment of its kind. He sent a bill afterwards; Mahler paid it.
entries.source_note: Freud's recollection (letter to Reik, 1935, and to Marie Bonaparte), written later.

entries.headline: 'What an autobiography': the Fifth Symphony at lunch
entries.digest: Three days after Mahler died in Vienna, Schnitzler walked with a friend over the Cobenzl to Grinzing, where Mahler would be buried the next day. At lunch with his mother they played and talked about Mahler's Fifth Symphony, and Schnitzler wrote that it read like an autobiography.
entries.source_note: Schnitzler Tagebuch 21 May 1911 (Tagebuch 1909–1912, p. 241, austriaca.at).

entries.headline: Painting Mahler's burial
entries.digest: Mahler was buried at Grinzing on 22 May 1911. Schoenberg, who had been there, afterwards painted the scene: a few dark figures at a grave under a heavy sky. A year later he would call Mahler a saint in a memorial lecture.
entries.source_note: Mahler Foundation, 'Arnold Schoenberg' (painting dated after 22-05-1911; memorial address March 1912).

entries.headline: The Watschenkonzert
entries.digest: Schoenberg conducted the Wiener Konzertverein in works by Webern, Zemlinsky, himself and Berg. Catcalls began after the second of Webern's pieces; during Berg's songs on picture-postcard texts by Peter Altenberg the hall erupted, and the organiser Erhard Buschbeck struck a heckler. The concert was abandoned before Mahler's Kindertotenlieder could be performed. The slap later went to court.
entries.source_note: Schenker Documents Online footnote (31 March 1913, ended early); Schnitzler Chronik event record (Buschbeck, Oscar Straus, Op. 9, Berg songs).

entries.headline: In the hall for the scandal
entries.digest: Schnitzler spent the day at a rehearsal of his Professor Bernhardi and in the evening went to the Musikverein concert. His diary names Schoenberg, Berg and his songs, and Mahler, whose songs never came. He was among the many prominent Viennese who later found themselves witnesses to the brawl.
entries.source_note: Schnitzler Chronik, 31 March 1913 (diary entry tags Berg, Schönberg, Mahler, the two orchestral songs, Musikverein; concert event links Schnitzler). Diary wording not checked.

entries.headline: The scandal as household news
entries.digest: Before nine in the morning a visitor came to tell Schenker's companion Lie-Liechen what had happened at the 'Schoenberg scandal' the night before. Schenker recorded the visit but not his own reaction; Vienna learned of the concert as gossip before the papers.
entries.source_note: Schenker diary, 1 April 1913 (OJ 1/12), Schenker Documents Online.

entries.place: Berlin; printed in Die Zeit, Vienna
entries.headline: Schoenberg answers from Berlin
entries.digest: Back in Berlin, Schoenberg gave a statement published in Die Zeit on 3 April. He blamed the whistlers for starting the trouble, attacked the press, said even the successful Gurrelieder had suffered from prejudice, and declared he would not take part in concerts unless disturbance were forbidden on the tickets.
entries.source_note: Arnold Schönberg Center, '1913 – Der Skandal im Konzertsaal' (Die Zeit, 3 April 1913).

entries.headline: Kokoschka, superstition and Freud at the Zuckerkandls'
entries.digest: Schnitzler dined at Berta Zuckerkandl's with Carl Moll and his wife. The talk ran over paintings, Kokoschka, superstition and Freud, and Schnitzler read poems by Christian Morgenstern aloud. It is an ordinary evening, and almost every name in this chapter is in the room or in the conversation.
entries.source_note: Schnitzler Tagebuch 21 Nov 1913 (Tagebuch 1913–1916, p. 77, austriaca.at).

entries.headline: The Gurrelieder at home
entries.digest: After a morning of dictation and a tax consultation, Schnitzler had music at home in the evening: Mussorgsky and Schoenberg's Gurrelieder. A year after the scandal concert, the early, lush Schoenberg was already domestic music in a writer's house.
entries.source_note: Schnitzler Tagebuch 17 March 1914 (Tagebuch 1913–1916, p. 104, austriaca.at).

entries.headline: A card from Brussels
entries.digest: Klimt sent Emilie Flöge a postcard from Brussels, where the Palais Stoclet, Hoffmann's house for the banker Adolphe Stoclet with Klimt's mosaic frieze in the dining room, had been finished. Six weeks later the heir to the throne was shot in Sarajevo.
entries.source_note: Klimt-Database biography (postcard 18 May 1914, Brussels); Stoclet 1905–1911 per MAK.

claims.claim: Nineteen artists found the Vienna Secession with Klimt as president
Olbrich's Secession building opens with the second exhibition and Hevesi's motto over the door
Die Traumdeutung is published, its title page dated 1900
claims.evidence: Jones, cited by History of Information

claims.claim: Philosophy shown at the 7th Secession exhibition; press war follows
87 professors petition against installing Philosophy; it wins a Grand Prix in Paris
Leutnant Gustl published in the Neue Freie Presse Christmas supplement
Mahler's six-trombone arrangement from Beethoven's Ninth performed at the Beethoven exhibition preview
Beethoven Frieze shown at the 14th exhibition; meant to be temporary, it is kept and sold
Wiener Werkstätte founded by Hoffmann, Moser and Waerndorfer
Bahr publishes Gegen Klimt, an anthology of the attacks
Klimt withdraws from the faculty commission and repays the fee; the Klimt group leaves the Secession (14 June)
Mahler leaves Vienna for New York; Klimt's reported 'Vorbei' is anecdote, not document
Kunstschau opens; the state buys The Kiss (shown as 'Liebespaar') for 25,000 crowns
Second String Quartet premiered amid laughter and whistling
claims.evidence: Schönberg Center timeline (year); day from standard accounts

claims.claim: Watschenkonzert at the Musikverein abandoned after riot; Buschbeck's slap later tried in court
claims.evidence: Schenker Documents Online; Schnitzler Chronik; Schönberg Center

convergences.label: The Secession building opens
convergences.note: Hevesi supplied the words over the door, Klimt the goddess inside, Hoffmann and his colleagues the rooms. Three makers of one building, each recording it in his own medium: a review, a painting, a design.

convergences.label: The Philosophy scandal, March–May 1900
convergences.note: The painter said almost nothing; Hevesi and Bahr defended him daily; Kraus mocked both the picture and its defenders. A few streets away Freud, whose dream book had just appeared, was writing to Berlin about the silence that met his own vision of the irrational.

convergences.label: Dinner at the Zuckerkandls'
convergences.note: Alma's diary is written that night; Mahler's side survives in the invitation he sent the next morning; the hostess's version was written in exile almost forty years later. Klimt, her earlier suitor, sat beside her.

convergences.label: The Beethoven exhibition opens
convergences.note: A Gesamtkunstwerk in practice: Hoffmann's rooms, Klimt's frieze, Klinger's statue and, for one evening, Mahler's trombones on the stairs. The critics' outrage at the frieze and the crowds of nearly 60,000 came together.

convergences.label: Mahler leaves Vienna
convergences.note: Mahler's own record is the farewell note of two days earlier; Klimt's single word survives only as anecdote. Alma was beside Mahler on the train.

convergences.label: Kunstschau 1908
convergences.note: The breakaways' own exhibition: Klimt's room, Moser's design, Zuckerkandl's reporting, and the state buying the painting it had refused to hang on the university ceiling.

convergences.label: Mahler's death and burial
convergences.note: Schnitzler listened to the Fifth and called it an autobiography; Schoenberg painted the grave. Two private responses, one in words and one in paint, three days apart.

convergences.label: The Watschenkonzert
convergences.note: The conductor, a diarist in the hall and a hostile theorist hearing it the next morning: three distances from the same riot.

ties.note: Klimt courted Alma in 1899 and travelled with her family through Italy; her stepfather broke it off.
Married 9 March 1902 after six weeks' courtship and a letter asking her to stop composing.
Zuckerkandl's dinner of 7 November 1901 introduced Alma to Mahler.
Schnitzler dined in her salon repeatedly; his diary records the talk.
Kraus had mocked Bahr in 'Die demolirte Literatur' (1896–97) and attacked him again in Die Fackel over the Klimt campaign.
Kraus wrote against Philosophy (1900) and Jurisprudence (1903) in Die Fackel.
Hevesi wrote the Secession's motto and reviewed nearly every Klimt showing on its opening day.
Bahr owned Nuda Veritas, lectured in Klimt's defence and published Gegen Klimt.
Leiden, late August 1910: a four-hour walk that Freud later counted as a brief analysis.
Each read the other's work closely; Schnitzler's monologues and dream notes ran parallel to Freud's method, and Freud later wrote to him as a kind of double.
Mahler championed Schoenberg from the mid-1900s; Schoenberg painted his burial and called him a saint.
Schenker's theory defended tonal tradition against everything Schoenberg's music did after 1908.
Partners from the Secession's founding through the 1905 walkout, the Kunstschau and the Palais Stoclet.
They met at Waerndorfer's in 1907 and through the Zuckerkandl and Moll households.

threads_out.note: Six weeks after Klimt's postcard from Brussels, Franz Ferdinand was killed at Sarajevo. Kraus turned the war into Die letzten Tage der Menschheit, Schnitzler kept his diary through it, and Schoenberg was called up in 1915.

Lise Meitner studied physics at the University of Vienna from 1901 to 1906, the years of the faculty-paintings dispute over the same university's Great Hall, and took her doctorate under Boltzmann's school before leaving for Berlin.

The Watschenkonzert of 31 March 1913 and the Paris premiere of The Rite of Spring on 29 May 1913 were the two great concert scandals of the same spring; Stravinsky had heard Schoenberg's Pierrot lunaire in Berlin a few months earlier.

The Wiener Werkstätte's union of art and craft was a forerunner of the Bauhaus, Kandinsky began writing to Schoenberg in January 1911, and Walter Gropius, whose affair with Alma sent Mahler to Freud in 1910, married her in 1915 and founded the Bauhaus in 1919.
The Secession brought French painting to Vienna, including a survey of the development of Impressionism in its 1903 exhibitions, three decades after the first Impressionist show in Paris.

images.caption: Period photograph of the first faculty painting, shown in March 1900. The original burned with the other faculty paintings at Schloss Immendorf in May 1945; only photographs remain.
